title: Oatmeal and honey cold-process soap
subtitle: A gentle bar for dry and sensitive skin
excerpt: A cold-process bar with rolled oats and a spoonful of honey stirred through the batter for a creamy, lightly exfoliating bar suited to dry or sensitive skin. The honey gives the bar a warm, golden tint and speeds saponification slightly. Makes 7 bars.
sourceNotes: Oatmeal in cold-process soap: general soapmaking reference. Honey in cold-process soap (sugars accelerating trace, heating effect): Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997). Note on honey in alkaline batter: the lye neutralises most of the honey's active compounds; the primary benefit in the finished bar is a slightly silky lather and the warm colour. SAP values from SoapCalc.

recipe.batchNotes: Run any scale change through a lye calculator.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Two years in a cool dark cupboard once cured. Honey soaps can be slightly more prone to overheating in the mould; if the bar develops a liquid pool around the oats, it has overheated during gel phase. This is cosmetic only. Discard if DOS or rancid smell develop.

glossaryTerms.definition: The reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide that produces soap and glycerine. Each oil has a SAP value: grams of lye per gram of oil.
The point at which soap batter thickens to thin-custard consistency. Honey and sugar accelerate trace; add them at trace and pour immediately.

The period during saponification when the soap batter heats internally, turning translucent from the centre outward. Honey accelerates gel phase; do not insulate honey soaps as heavily as unscented bars to prevent overheating.

projectSchedule.title: Unmould and cut
projectSchedule.body: Turn out the loaf. The bar should be a warm golden-tan colour from the honey. The oats will be visible in the cut face. Wear protective gloves.

projectSchedule.title: Turn the bars
projectSchedule.body: Flip each bar. The golden tone may deepen slightly as the bar matures.

projectSchedule.title: Four-week test
projectSchedule.body: Test a sliver. No sting means safe. The bar is ready to use; the oats exfoliate gently in use.

projectSchedule.title: Cure complete
projectSchedule.body: A fully cured oatmeal honey bar is firm and golden, with a creamy, stable lather.

content.text: Method
Mix lye solution

In a ventilated space with protective gloves and goggles on, add the sodium hydroxide to the distilled water. Stir until dissolved. Cool to 35 to 40°C (slightly cooler than standard, to reduce overheating risk with honey).
Prepare oils and oats

Melt coconut oil and shea butter. Add olive oil and castor oil. Cool to 35 to 40°C. Blend the rolled oats briefly in a dry blender to break them into coarser pieces (full whole oats can scratch the skin). Set aside.
Blend to trace and add oats and honey

Pour the lye solution into the oils. Blend to light trace. Dissolve the honey in one teaspoon of warm water, then stir it into the batter at trace along with the ground oats. Pour immediately as honey accelerates the batter.
Mould and cure

Pour into the silicone mould. Insulate lightly with a single towel; do not use a heavy insulation box as honey soaps can overheat. Check after one hour: if the mould feels hot, remove the towel. Leave 48 hours. Unmould wearing protective gloves. Cut and cure 4 to 6 weeks.
Storage and shelf life
Two years in a cool dark cupboard. The golden tone deepens very slightly over time. Discard if DOS or rancid smell appear.
